q: A straight wire of length 1.0 m is placed along x -axis, in a region with magnetic field B→=(3i^+2j^)T. A current of 2.0 A flows in the wire along +x direction. The magnetic force acting on the wire is :
subject: physics
exp:
Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Wire

The magnetic force (\(\vec{F}\)) on a straight wire of length \(L\) carrying a current \(I\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is given by the formula:
\(\vec{F} = I (\vec{L} \times \vec{B})\)

Current: \(I = 2.0 \text{ A}\)
Length: \(L = 1.0 \text{ m}\)
Magnetic Field: \(\vec{B} = (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \text{ T}\)
Length Vector (\(\vec{L}\) is along \(+x\) direction): \(\vec{L} = L\hat{i} = (1.0 \text{ m})\hat{i}\)
Calculation

Step 1: Calculate the cross product \(\vec{L} \times \vec{B}\)
\(\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = (1.0\hat{i}) \times (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})\)
\(\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = 3(\hat{i} \times \hat{i}) + 2(\hat{i} \times \hat{j})\)
Since \(\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = 0\) and \(\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}\):
\(\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = 0 + 2\hat{k}\)
\(\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = 2\hat{k} \text{ T}\cdot\text{m}\)

Step 2: Calculate the force \(\vec{F}\)
\(\vec{F} = I (\vec{L} \times \vec{B})\)
\(\vec{F} = (2.0 \text{ A}) (2\hat{k} \text{ T}\cdot\text{m})\)
\(\vec{F} = 4.0\hat{k} \text{ N}\)

Final Answer
The magnitude of the force is \(4.0 \text{ N}\) and the direction is along the \(\textbf{+z-axis}\).

This corresponds to Option C.

q: Let π2<x<π be such that cotx=-511. Then sin11x2(sin6x-cos6x)+cos11x2(sin6x+cos6x) is equal to
subject: maths
exp:
1. Simplify the trigonometric expression

Let the given expression be EE.

E=(sin⁡11x2)(sin⁡6x−cos⁡6x)+(cos⁡11x2)(sin⁡6x+cos⁡6x)E = \left(\sin \frac{11x}{2}\right)(\sin 6x - \cos 6x) + \left(\cos \frac{11x}{2}\right)(\sin 6x + \cos 6x)

Expand the terms:

E=sin⁡11x2sin⁡6x−sin⁡11x2cos⁡6x+cos⁡11x2sin⁡6x+cos⁡11x2cos⁡6xE = \sin \frac{11x}{2} \sin 6x - \sin \frac{11x}{2} \cos 6x + \cos \frac{11x}{2} \sin 6x + \cos \frac{11x}{2} \cos 6x

Rearrange the terms to group familiar identities:

E=(cos⁡11x2cos⁡6x+sin⁡11x2sin⁡6x)+(cos⁡11x2sin⁡6x−sin⁡11x2cos⁡6x)E = \left(\cos \frac{11x}{2} \cos 6x + \sin \frac{11x}{2} \sin 6x\right) + \left(\cos \frac{11x}{2} \sin 6x - \sin \frac{11x}{2} \cos 6x\right)

We recognize the cosine difference formula

cos⁡(A−B)=cos⁡Acos⁡B+sin⁡Asin⁡B\cos(A-B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B and

the sine difference formula

sin⁡(B−A)=sin⁡Bcos⁡A−cos⁡Bsin⁡A\sin(B-A) = \sin B \cos A - \cos B \sin A.

Let A=11x2A = \frac{11x}{2} and B=6xB = 6x.

The first part is cos⁡(11x2−6x)\cos\left(\frac{11x}{2} - 6x\right).

The second part is sin⁡(6x−11x2)\sin\left(6x - \frac{11x}{2}\right).

Calculate the arguments:

A−B=11x2−12x2=−x2A - B = \frac{11x}{2} - \frac{12x}{2} = -\frac{x}{2}

B−A=12x2−11x2=x2B - A = \frac{12x}{2} - \frac{11x}{2} = \frac{x}{2}

Substitute these back into the expression:

E=cos⁡(−x2)+sin⁡(x2)E = \cos\left(-\frac{x}{2}\right) + \sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Given:} \\
&I = 0.5~\mathrm{A}, \quad \vec{L} = 1~\mathrm{cm} = 0.01~\hat{i}~\mathrm{m}, \\
&\vec{B} = (0.4~\mathrm{mT})~\hat{j} + (0.6~\mathrm{mT})~\hat{k} = (0.4 \times 10^{-3})~\hat{j} + (0.6 \times 10^{-3})~\hat{k} \\[6pt]
&\text{Magnetic force: } \vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B}) \\[6pt]
&\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = (0.01\hat{i}) \times \left[(0.4\times10^{-3})\hat{j} + (0.6\times10^{-3})\hat{k}\right] \\[6pt]
&= 0.01\left[(0.4\times10^{-3})(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}) + (0.6\times10^{-3})(\hat{i}\times\hat{k})\right] \\[6pt]
&\text{Since } \hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k} \text{ and } \hat{i}\times\hat{k} = -\hat{j}, \\[4pt]
&\vec{L}\times\vec{B} = 0.01\left[(0.4\times10^{-3})\hat{k} - (0.6\times10^{-3})\hat{j}\right] \\[6pt]
&= (4\times10^{-6})\hat{k} - (6\times10^{-6})\hat{j} \\[6pt]
&\therefore \vec{F} = I(\vec{L}\times\vec{B}) = 0.5\left[(4\times10^{-6})\hat{k} - (6\times10^{-6})\hat{j}\right] \\[6pt]
&\boxed{\vec{F} = (-3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})~\mu\mathrm{N}}
\end{aligned}
\]

Magnetic field B is along +z.
Each small current element Idl on the loop experiences

F =Idl×B
Since the loop lies in the zy-plane, B (along z) is perpendicular to some elements and parallel to others.
For an element where current flows along +y,F =Idl×B is along +x.
For the opposite element (current along -y ), F is along -x.
These forces act outward on opposite sides - tending to pull the loop outward.
Hence, the loop experiences an outward (radial) magnetic pressure.

q:
A solid cylinder of mass \(m\) and radius \(r\) is released from rest at the top of a rough inclined plane making an angle of \(45^{\circ}\) with the horizontal. Assuming the cylinder rolls without slipping, find the acceleration of the axis of the cylinder.

(Shift I - Memory Based)
subject: physics
exp:
Given:
  • Mass of the cylinder: mm
  • Radius of the cylinder: rr
  • Inclined plane angle: θ=45∘\theta = 45^\circ
Steps:

  1. Forces acting on the cylinder:

    • Component of gravitational force along the incline: mgsin⁡θm g \sin \theta
    • Frictional force: ff
    • Normal force: N=mgcos⁡θN = m g \cos \theta

  2. Equations of motion: For rolling without slipping:

    • Translational motion: ma=mgsin⁡θ−fm a = m g \sin \theta - f
    • Rotational motion about the center of mass: fr=Iαf r = I \alpha For a solid cylinder, I=12mr2I = \frac{1}{2} m r^2, and rolling without slipping implies α=ar\alpha = \frac{a}{r}.
      Substituting II and α\alpha: fr=12mr2⋅arf r = \frac{1}{2} m r^2 \cdot \frac{a}{r},​ f=12maf = \frac{1}{2} m a

  3. Substitute ff into the translational motion equation:

    ma=mgsin⁡θ−12mam a = m g \sin \theta - \frac{1}{2} m a

    Simplify:

    ma+12ma=mgsin⁡θm a + \frac{1}{2} m a = m g \sin \theta, 32ma=mgsin⁡θ\frac{3}{2} m a = m g \sin \theta, a=23gsin⁡θa = \frac{2}{3} g \sin \theta

  4. Substitute θ=45∘\theta = 45^\circ:

    a=23gsin⁡45∘a = \frac{2}{3} g \sin 45^\circ

    Since sin⁡45∘=12\sin 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}

    a=23g⋅12=2g32a = \frac{2}{3} g \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2g}{3\sqrt{2}}​
Final Answer:

The acceleration of the axis of the cylinder is:

a=2g32a = \frac{2g}{3\sqrt{2}}​

q: You are required to design an air-filled solenoid of inductance 0.016 H having a length 0.81 m and radius 0.02 m . The number of turns in the solenoid should be

we use the formula for the number of turns per unit length of a solenoid:

\[L=\mu_0 n^2 A l\]

q: In a metre-bridge when a resistance in the left gap is \(2 \Omega\) and unknown resistance in the right gap, the balance length is found to be \(40\) cm. On shunting the unknown resistance with \(2 \Omega\), the balance length changes by:EndFragment

Let the unknown resistance in the right gap be \(R\). By the meter bridge principle:

\(\frac{2}{40}=\frac{R}{100-40}\Longrightarrow \frac{2}{40}=\frac{R}{60}\Longrightarrow R=3\Omega\)

When \(R\) is shunted (in parallel) with \(2\Omega\), the new right gap resistance is:

& \text{Given: Galvanometer resistance } = G\ \Omega, \quad \text{Full-scale current } = I\ \mathrm{A}, \\[3pt]
& \text{Current through galvanometer } = 0.1\% \text{ of } I = \frac{0.1}{100}I = \frac{I}{1000}. \\[6pt]
& \text{Let shunt resistance } = S. \text{ Then the same potential difference acts across } G \text{ and } S. \\[3pt]
& \text{So, } I_g G = I_s S, \quad \text{where } I_s = I - I_g = I - \frac{I}{1000} = \frac{999I}{1000}. \\[4pt]
& \Rightarrow S = \frac{I_g G}{I_s} = \frac{\frac{I}{1000} G}{\frac{999I}{1000}} = \frac{G}{999}. \\[6pt]
& \text{The equivalent resistance of the ammeter is } R_A = G \parallel S \\[4pt]
& R_A = \frac{G \times S}{G + S} = \frac{G \times \frac{G}{999}}{G + \frac{G}{999}} = \frac{G^2 / 999}{G(1 + 1/999)} \\[4pt]
& R_A = \frac{G / 999}{1 + 1/999} = \frac{G / 999}{1000/999} = \frac{G}{1000}. \\[6pt]
& \boxed{R_A = \frac{G}{1000}} \\[4pt]
& \text{Hence, the resistance of the ammeter is } \boxed{\tfrac{G}{1000}\ \Omega.}
\end{aligned}

q: A spring-block system has a time period of 2 seconds. If D is the total distance traveled by the block and \(d\) is the displacement of the block in 12.5 seconds, find the ratio D/d.(Shift I - Memory Based)
subject: physics
exp:
1. Key concepts:

    • The total distance DD is the sum of all oscillations' displacements (absolute values of motion).
    • Displacement ddd is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions.
    • The time period T=2 sT = 2 \, \text{s}.

  2. Oscillation in 12.5 seconds:

    • Number of complete oscillations: n=Total timeTime period=12.52=6.25n = \frac{\text{Total time}}{\text{Time period}} = \frac{12.5}{2} = 6.25
    • This implies 6 full oscillations and 1/4 of another oscillation.

  3. Displacement (dd):

    • After 6 full oscillations, the block returns to its starting position.
    • During the remaining 0.25×T=0.5 s0.25 \times T = 0.5 \, \text{s}, the block moves from the mean position to the maximum displacement (amplitude AA).
    • Hence, d=Ad = A

  4. Total distance (DD):

    • In one complete oscillation, the block covers a distance of 4A4A(2A forward and 2A backward).
    • For 6 complete oscillations: D6 oscillations=6⋅4A=24AD_{\text{6 oscillations}} = 6 \cdot 4A = 24A
    • In the last quarter oscillation: Dlast quarter=AD_{\text{last quarter}} = A
    • Total distance: D=D6 oscillations+Dlast quarter=24A+A=25AD = D_{\text{6 oscillations}} + D_{\text{last quarter}} = 24A + A = 25A

  5. Ratio Dd\frac{D}{d}​:

    Dd=25AA=25\frac{D}{d} = \frac{25A}{A} = 25

Answer: Dd=25\frac{D}{d} = 25

q: A straight wire of length 1.0 m is placed along x -axis, in a region with magnetic field B→=(3i^+2j^)T. A current of 2.0 A flows in the wire along +x direction. The magnetic force acting on the wire is :
subject: physics
exp:
Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Wire

The magnetic force (\(\vec{F}\)) on a straight wire of length \(L\) carrying a current \(I\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is given by the formula:
\(\vec{F} = I (\vec{L} \times \vec{B})\)

Current: \(I = 2.0 \text{ A}\)
Length: \(L = 1.0 \text{ m}\)
Magnetic Field: \(\vec{B} = (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \text{ T}\)
Length Vector (\(\vec{L}\) is along \(+x\) direction): \(\vec{L} = L\hat{i} = (1.0 \text{ m})\hat{i}\)
Calculation

Step 1: Calculate the cross product \(\vec{L} \times \vec{B}\)
\(\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = (1.0\hat{i}) \times (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})\)
\(\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = 3(\hat{i} \times \hat{i}) + 2(\hat{i} \times \hat{j})\)
Since \(\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = 0\) and \(\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}\):
\(\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = 0 + 2\hat{k}\)
\(\vec{L} \times \vec{B} = 2\hat{k} \text{ T}\cdot\text{m}\)

Step 2: Calculate the force \(\vec{F}\)
\(\vec{F} = I (\vec{L} \times \vec{B})\)
\(\vec{F} = (2.0 \text{ A}) (2\hat{k} \text{ T}\cdot\text{m})\)
\(\vec{F} = 4.0\hat{k} \text{ N}\)

Final Answer
The magnitude of the force is \(4.0 \text{ N}\) and the direction is along the \(\textbf{+z-axis}\).

This corresponds to Option C.

q: Two particles A and B of the same mass but having charges q and 4q respectively, are accelerated from rest through different potential differences VA and VB such that they attain same kinetic energies. The value of VAVB is :
subject: physics
exp:
The kinetic energy (\(KE\)) gained by a charged particle when accelerated through a potential difference (\(V\)) is given by the formula:
\(KE = qV\)
where \(q\) is the charge of the particle.

For particle A with charge \(q\) and potential difference \(V_A\):
\(KE_A = qV_A\)
For particle B with charge \(4q\) and potential difference \(V_B\):
\(KE_B = 4qV_B\)
Since both particles attain the same kinetic energy, we can equate the expressions:
\(qV_A = 4qV_B\)

We can divide both sides of the equation by \(q\) (assuming \(q \neq 0\)):
\(V_A = 4V_B\)

Now, we can express the ratio of the potential differences:
\(\frac{V_A}{V_B} = 4\)

The value of \(\left(\frac{V_A}{V_B}\right)\) is 4.

Thus, the answer is (D) 4.

q: A voltage v=v0 sin ωt applied to a circuit drives a current i=i0sin (ωt+ϕ) in the circuit. The average power consumed in the circuit over a cycle is
subject: physics
exp:
To find the average power consumed in the circuit, we begin with the instantaneous power, which is the product of the voltage

\(v(t)\)and the current\(i(t)\)

:

\[p(t)=v(t) \cdot i(t)=\left(v_0 \sin (\omega t)\right) \cdot\left(i_0 \sin (\omega t+\phi)\right)\] \[\sin A \sin B=\frac{1}{2}[\cos (A-B)-\cos (A+B)]\] \[\sin (\omega t) \sin (\omega t+\phi)=\frac{1}{2}[\cos (-\phi)-\cos (2 \omega t+\phi)]\] \[\cos (-\phi)=\cos (\phi)\]

, thus:

\[p(t)=v_0 i_0 \frac{1}{2}[\cos (\phi)-\cos (2 \omega t+\phi)]\]

To find the average power over a cycle, integrate this expression over one period

\[T=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}\]

, then divide by

\[T\]

:

\[P_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T v_0 i_0 \frac{1}{2}[\cos (\phi)-\cos (2 \omega t+\phi)] d t\]

This separates into two integrals:

\[P_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{v_0 i_0}{2 T}\left[\int_0^T \cos (\phi) d t-\int_0^T \cos (2 \omega t+\phi) d t\right]\] \[P_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{v_0 i_0}{2 T}\left[\int_0^T \cos (\phi) d t-\int_0^T \cos (2 \omega t+\phi) d t\right]\]

\(2 = \sqrt{2.0 \times \epsilon_r}\) \(\Longrightarrow\) \(4 = 2.0 \times \epsilon_r\) \(\Longrightarrow\) \(\epsilon_r = 2\).

q: A galvanometer of resistance \(G \Omega\) is converted into an ammeter of range 0 to IA. If the current through the galvanometer is \(0.1 \%\) of I A, the resistance of the ammeter is :
subject: physics
exp:
\begin{aligned}
& \text{Given: Galvanometer resistance } = G\ \Omega, \quad \text{Full-scale current } = I\ \mathrm{A}, \\[3pt]
& \text{Current through galvanometer } = 0.1\% \text{ of } I = \frac{0.1}{100}I = \frac{I}{1000}. \\[6pt]
& \text{Let shunt resistance } = S. \text{ Then the same potential difference acts across } G \text{ and } S. \\[3pt]
& \text{So, } I_g G = I_s S, \quad \text{where } I_s = I - I_g = I - \frac{I}{1000} = \frac{999I}{1000}. \\[4pt]
& \Rightarrow S = \frac{I_g G}{I_s} = \frac{\frac{I}{1000} G}{\frac{999I}{1000}} = \frac{G}{999}. \\[6pt]
& \text{The equivalent resistance of the ammeter is } R_A = G \parallel S \\[4pt]
& R_A = \frac{G \times S}{G + S} = \frac{G \times \frac{G}{999}}{G + \frac{G}{999}} = \frac{G^2 / 999}{G(1 + 1/999)} \\[4pt]
& R_A = \frac{G / 999}{1 + 1/999} = \frac{G / 999}{1000/999} = \frac{G}{1000}. \\[6pt]
& \boxed{R_A = \frac{G}{1000}} \\[4pt]
& \text{Hence, the resistance of the ammeter is } \boxed{\tfrac{G}{1000}\ \Omega.}
\end{aligned}

q:
A balloon of mass M is ascending with an acceleration a. What fraction of its mass should be dropped so that it starts moving upward with an acceleration of 3 a ?

(Shift - II Memory Based)
subject: physics
exp:
Let:

  • MM be the initial mass of the balloon.
  • TT be the tension (upward force) acting on the balloon.
Step 1: Initial Equation of Motion

Using Newton’s second law for the initial state:

T−Mg=MaT - Mg = Ma

T=M(g+a)T = M(g + a)

Step 2: After Dropping Mass

Let mm be the mass that is dropped. The new mass of the balloon becomes (M−m)(M - m). The equation of motion after dropping mass:

T−(M−m)g=(M−m)⋅3aT - (M - m)g = (M - m) \cdot 3a

Substituting T=M(g+a)T = M(g + a):

M(g+a)−(M−m)g=(M−m)⋅3aM(g + a) - (M - m)g = (M - m) \cdot 3a

Expanding:

Mg+Ma−Mg+mg=3a(M−m)Mg + Ma - Mg + mg = 3a(M - m)

Ma+mg=3aM−3amMa + mg = 3aM - 3am

Rearrange terms:

Ma−3aM=−mg−3amMa - 3aM = - mg - 3am

Ma−3aM=−m(g+3a)Ma - 3aM = -m(g + 3a)

Step 3: Solve for mm

m=2aMg+3am = \frac{2aM}{g + 3a}​

Answer:

The mass that should be dropped is 2aMg+3a\frac{2aM}{g+3a}.

q: A point object is placed in air at a distance of 4R on the principal axis of a convex spherical surface of radius of curvature R separating two mediums, air and glass. As the object is moved towards the surface, the image formed is :
subject: physics
exp:
To determine the nature of the image formed by a convex spherical surface separating air and glass, we need to consider the refraction of light at the convex surface. The nature of the image (real or virtual) depends on the position of the object relative to the focal point of the convex surface.


Identify the given parameters: object distance (\(u = -4R\)), radius of curvature (\(R\)), and the refractive indices of air (\(n1 = 1\)) and glass (\(n2 > 1\)).

Use the refraction formula for a spherical surface:
\(\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\)
where \(u\) is the object distance, \(v\) is the image distance, and \(R\) is the radius of curvature.

Substitute the given values into the formula:
\(\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{1}{-4R} = \frac{n_2 - 1}{R}\)

Solve for the image distance \(v\). As the object moves towards the surface (\(u\) increases from \(-4R\) to \(0\)), analyze how the image distance \(v\) changes. Initially, when the object is far (\(u = -4R\)), the image is virtual. As the object moves closer to the surface, the image becomes real when the object is within the focal length of the convex surface.

Final Answer:
D. first real and then virtual

q:
A horizontal pipe of variable cross-section has a fluid of density ρ\rho flowing through it. At cross-sections A and B, the velocities are VAV_A​ and VBV_B, and the pressures are PAP_A​ and PBP_B​. Find the correct relation between velocities.

(Shift - II Memory Based)​
subject: physics
exp:
This question is based on Bernoulli's equation, which states:

P+12ρV2+ρgh=constantP + \frac{1}{2} \rho V^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}

Since the pipe is horizontal (hhh is constant), the equation simplifies to:

P+12ρV2=constantP + \frac{1}{2} \rho V^2 = \text{constant}

For points A and B:

PA+12ρVA2=PB+12ρVB2P_A + \frac{1}{2} \rho V_A^2 = P_B + \frac{1}{2} \rho V_B^2​

Rearranging:

12ρVA2−12ρVB2=PB−PA, ​ ρ2(VA2−VB2)=PB−PA​

Divide through by ρ/2\rho/2:

VA2−VB2=2(PB−PA)ρ​ Final Relation:

The correct option is:

VA2−VB2=2(PB−PA)ρ

q: A 10 cm long wire lies along y-axis. It carries a current of 1.0 A in positive y-direction. A magnetic field \(\vec{B}=(5 mT ) \hat{j}-(8 mT ) \hat{k}\) exists in the region. The force on the wire is :
subject: physics
exp:
\begin{aligned}
& \text{Given: } L = 10\ \text{cm} = 0.1\ \text{m}, \quad I = 1.0\ \text{A} \\[4pt]
& \text{Direction of current: along } +\hat{j} \\[2pt]
& \text{Magnetic field: } \vec{B} = (5\ \text{mT})\hat{j} - (8\ \text{mT})\hat{k}
= (5\times10^{-3})\hat{j} - (8\times10^{-3})\hat{k} \\[4pt]
& \text{Force on wire: } \vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B}) \\[4pt]
& \vec{L} = (0.1)\hat{j} \\[4pt]
& \Rightarrow \vec{F} = 1 \times \left[(0.1)\hat{j} \times \left(5\times10^{-3}\hat{j} - 8\times10^{-3}\hat{k}\right)\right] \\[4pt]
& \hat{j} \times \hat{j} = 0,\quad \hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i} \\[4pt]
& \Rightarrow \vec{F} = 0.1 \left[ -8\times10^{-3} (\hat{j} \times \hat{k}) \right]
= 0.1 \left[ -8\times10^{-3} \hat{i} \right] \\[4pt]
& \Rightarrow \vec{F} = -8\times10^{-4}\ \hat{i}\ \mathrm{N} \\[4pt]
& \text{Hence, the force on the wire is directed along } -x\text{-axis.} \\[6pt]
& \boxed{\vec{F} = -0.8\times10^{-3}\ \hat{i}\ \mathrm{N}}
\end{aligned}

exp:
The concentration of antimony (Sb) is given as 1 ppm (part per million) of the silicon atoms.The concentration of silicon atoms is 5×1028 m-35 cross 10 to the 28th power m to the negative 3 power. The concentration of antimony atoms, which act as donors (Ndcap N sub d), is calculated as:
